findings.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:13 — `match_count += 1` followed by `save` is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so concurrent validations can overwrite increments and produce inaccurate match statistics
lib/validators/email_validator.rb:20 — The domain restriction regex is not end-anchored, allowing domains such as `example.com.attacker.org` to bypass the configured registration allowlist

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

per_golden_matches.matched_candidate: app/models/blocked_email.rb:13 — `match_count += 1` followed by `save` is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so concurrent validations can overwrite increments and produce inaccurate match statistics
per_golden_matches.reasoning: Both comments identify the same underlying issue: the `should_block_email?` method has problematic side effects with `match_count += 1` and `save`. The golden comment focuses on the broader concern of side effects during a read operation and race conditions, while the candidate specifically identifies the non-atomic read-modify-write pattern causing race conditions. Both point to the same code problem - concurrent access issues with the counter increment in what should be a query method.

per_golden_matches.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
per_golden_matches.matched_candidate: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:20 — The domain restriction regex is not end-anchored, allowing domains such as `example.com.attacker.org` to bypass the configured registration allowlist
per_golden_matches.reasoning: Both comments identify the same underlying security issue: the domain restriction regex lacks proper anchoring, allowing bypass of the allowlist. The golden comment describes bypassing 'example.com' with 'evil.example.com' (subdomain attack), while the candidate describes bypassing with 'example.com.attacker.org' (suffix attack). Both are pointing to the same regex anchoring vulnerability in the email_in_restriction_setting? method that allows domain restriction bypass, just with slightly different attack vector examples. The core issue - improper regex anchoring allowing allowlist bypass - is identical.
